title: Peer Gynt Suite No. 1
hook: A sunrise, a deathbed, a seductive dance and a hall full of trolls, four scenes from Ibsen’s play about a Norwegian dreamer.

painting.title: Soria Moria Palace
painting.pairingNote: The fairy-tale palace of Soria Moria glowing at sunrise above the mist, by the painter of Norway’s trolls; in the play, Peer comforts his dying mother with an imaginary sleigh ride to this very castle.

facts: Henrik Ibsen wrote *Peer Gynt* in 1867 as a play in verse, about a boastful Norwegian country lad who lives in his own fantasies. Peer runs off with another man’s bride, wanders into the hall of the troll king, comes home in time for his mother’s death, and spends years abroad as a trader and a false prophet, while Solveig, the woman who loves him, waits.

When the play was to be staged, Ibsen asked Grieg in 1874 for [[incidental-music|incidental music]]. Grieg found it hard going and called the subject “terribly unmanageable”. The production opened in Christiania (now Oslo) on 24 February 1876, with about 90 minutes of his music, and was a great success.

More than ten years later Grieg chose four numbers for a concert suite, published in 1888, and a second suite followed in 1893. The four pieces are not in the play’s order: the sunrise comes from Act IV, Åse’s death from Act III, Anitra’s dance from Act IV, and the trolls from Act II.
“Morning” sounds like a Norwegian dawn to most listeners, but in the play the sun rises over the Moroccan desert, where Peer has been robbed and abandoned.
bigPicture.inOneLine: sunrise (I), a mother’s death (II), a dancer’s charm (III), a troll chase that ends in uproar (IV).

movements.heading: Morning Mood
movements.title: Morning Mood
movements.summary: A flute and an oboe pass a simple, rocking melody back and forth, like two birds greeting the light. The melody travels through new keys, grows warmer, and the whole orchestra blazes out as the sun breaks through. Unusually, this climax comes early; the rest of the piece is the calm of a bright morning.

mainIdeas.name: The melody
mainIdeas.description: five notes rising and falling in a gentle rocking rhythm, built on the [[pentatonic-scale|pentatonic scale]], first on the flute, then on the oboe.

stops.hear: A flute plays a gentle, rocking tune; an oboe answers with the same tune
stops.happening: First light. The melody alternates between flute and oboe

stops.hear: The tune moves into new keys, as if the light is changing
The strings take the tune and the whole orchestra swells to its loudest
stops.happening: The sun breaks through: the climax, very early

stops.hear: The cellos sing the melody, warm and full
A horn plays the tune softly
stops.happening: The melody in a new colour

stops.hear: Quick trills in the woodwinds, like birdsong

stops.label: Last 30 seconds
stops.hear: Soft, sustained chords; the flute and horn have the last word

notice: The loudest moment comes in the first minute or so. Notice how the rest of the piece stays bright but calm, as if the day has simply begun.

notes.title: In this recording
notes.body: This is Karajan’s digital recording with the Berlin Philharmonic, made in the Philharmonie in Berlin and released in 1983; he had recorded the suites with the same orchestra once before, in 1971. On the Spotify album Suite No. 1 is tracks 1–4, followed by Suite No. 2 and Sibelius’s *Pelléas et Mélisande*.

movements.heading: The Death of Åse
movements.title: The Death of Åse
movements.summary: Åse, Peer’s mother, is dying. Peer, home again, sits at her bed and pretends to drive her by sleigh to the fairy-tale castle of Soria Moria, where the king is giving a feast. By the time they reach the gate, she has died. The music is for strings alone: a slow, grieving phrase in B minor, repeated higher and louder, then sinking back into near silence.

mainIdeas.name: The lament
mainIdeas.description: a slow, heavy phrase that climbs a little and falls back, in hushed strings.

stops.hear: The strings play a slow, grieving phrase, very softly
The same phrase, higher and louder
The fullest, loudest moment, then the phrase begins to fall
The music sinks lower and grows softer

stops.label: Last minute
stops.hear: Very quiet, slow chords that almost disappear

notice: There are no winds, brass or drums here, only strings. Notice how much grief Grieg gets from a single phrase played again and again at different heights and volumes.

movements.heading: Anitra's Dance
movements.title: Anitra's Dance
movements.summary: In the desert Peer is taken for a prophet by a Bedouin tribe, and the chief’s daughter, Anitra, dances for him. She will soon run off with his money and his rings. Grieg writes a light, teasing mazurka for strings with a triangle.

mainIdeas.name: The dance
mainIdeas.description: a lilting, coquettish tune in the violins, in three beats, with little turns and sighs.

stops.hear: Light plucked chords, then a delicate tune in the violins; a triangle tinkles
stops.happening: Anitra’s dance begins, in A minor. The plucking is [[pizzicato|pizzicato]]

stops.hear: The tune changes direction, more sinuous and pleading
The first tune returns

stops.label: Last 15 seconds
stops.hear: The dance fades to a soft, plucked ending

notice: Listen for the triangle. It is the only instrument besides the strings, and it gives the dance its glint of jewellery.

movements.heading: In the Hall of the Mountain King
movements.title: In the Hall of the Mountain King
movements.summary: Peer has ridden into the hall of the troll king, the Dovre King, with the king’s daughter, and the troll courtiers shout for his blood. A short, sneaking tune starts very quietly in the lowest instruments, climbs, gets louder and faster, and ends in uproar. In the play the trolls sing; in the suite the music is for orchestra alone.

mainIdeas.name: The trolls’ tune
mainIdeas.description: a short, tiptoeing melody that is repeated again and again, a little higher each time, faster and louder.

stops.hear: Very softly, low plucked strings and bassoons creep through a short tune
stops.happening: The trolls stir, in B minor

stops.hear: The tune moves higher, to the violins, and keeps repeating
stops.happening: The same tune in a higher key

stops.hear: Louder and faster; the brass join in
Very fast and very loud, with crashing cymbals and drums

stops.label: Last 15 seconds
stops.hear: Huge, hammered chords and a final crash

notice: The tune never changes: only its speed, volume and register do. It is one long [[crescendo|crescendo]] and acceleration.

Grieg wrote to a friend that this piece reeked of ultra-Norwegianism and troll self-satisfaction, and that he could not bear to hear it, though he hoped the irony would come through. It became one of his best-known pieces.

threads.title: A play without words
threads.body: Each piece is a scene from Ibsen, with the actors removed. Knowing the story (a sunrise in the desert, a mother’s deathbed and her imaginary sleigh ride, a dancer who robs her admirer, a troll hall) changes what you hear.

threads.title: Order of a concert, not of the play
threads.body: Grieg arranged the scenes for contrast: calm, grief, charm, fury. The suite ends with its loudest number, as a concert piece should.

threads.title: Simple tunes, big effects
threads.body: Every piece is built from one short melody, repeated and recoloured. Grieg’s skill is in the orchestra: flute and oboe, hushed strings, a triangle, a crescendo.
